method.scope: Current first-party employer role pages, employer-controlled job boards, official occupational context, and official AI risk guidance.
method.source_policy: Primary sources only for material role claims; no job aggregators, anonymous role summaries, or training-vendor definitions.
method.currentness_note: Job postings are volatile and the 2026 sample is unusually LLM/agent-heavy. Durable conclusions require convergence across employers and industries and must not turn a current model family or framework into the role definition.

sources.title: Applied AI Engineer, Codex Core Agent
sources.evidence_summary: Defines an applied AI engineer as closing the gap between research capability and real usefulness through agent behavior, real-task evaluation, prompting/tool/context experiments, production failure analysis, data/feedback loops, and product collaboration.
sources.limitations: One frontier-lab product and an agent/coding specialization; its model access and product context are not universal.

sources.title: OpenAI careers - Applied AI Engineering
sources.evidence_summary: Shows an Applied AI Engineering organization and multiple current Applied AI Engineer, Applied AI Software Engineer, product, evaluation, data, integrity, performance, infrastructure, and vertical specializations.
sources.limitations: Internal organization names are broader than one occupation and change with organizational structure.

sources.title: Applied AI Engineer
sources.evidence_summary: Calls for hands-on software engineering that translates frontier research into scalable AI product features, prototypes and evaluates methods, builds multimodal/agent pipelines, and partners with platform engineers to productionize SDKs and APIs.
sources.limitations: Business-operations and agentic emphasis in one large consumer-technology employer.

sources.title: Applied AI Engineer - AI Infrastructure
sources.evidence_summary: Uses the exact title for AI infrastructure that changes engineering and product-development work, demonstrating that applied AI can target internal systems as well as external user features.
sources.limitations: The visible page is JavaScript-backed and the specialization is internal engineering infrastructure.

sources.title: Anthropic careers catalog
sources.evidence_summary: Lists Applied AI Engineer roles across general, beneficial-deployment, enterprise, and life-sciences contexts while separately listing Applied AI Architect, Solutions Architect, Forward Deployed Engineer, research, infrastructure, and safety roles.
sources.limitations: A career catalog proves organizational separation and title use, not the complete responsibility model for each requisition.

sources.title: Applied AI Engineer, Global Public Sector
sources.evidence_summary: Requires applied AI engineers to frame public-sector problems, build and deploy end-to-end AI applications, create datasets, design evaluation frameworks, fine-tune models, collaborate cross-functionally, and share capability.
sources.limitations: Customer-facing public-sector role overlaps strongly with FDE; the broader title cannot be defined by this engagement model alone.

sources.title: Applied AI Engineer - Agentic Workflows
sources.evidence_summary: Frames an agentic specialization that owns design, build, deployment, evaluation, post-deployment iteration, reliability, observability, safety, auditability, customer collaboration, and shared platform standards.
sources.limitations: Explicitly an agentic and customer-facing specialization; it supports but does not exhaust the general Applied AI Engineer role.

sources.title: Applied AI Engineer
sources.evidence_summary: Defines a hands-on product role owning concept-to-production AI features, real-user validation, experimentation, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, continuous improvement, reliability, latency, cost, tool/API integration, and cross-functional delivery.
sources.limitations: Health/wellness product and current LLM-agent stack; formal clinical authority is not assigned to the role.

sources.title: Applied AI Engineer
sources.evidence_summary: Assigns full-lifecycle clinical AI workflow engineering: retrieval, reasoning, tool use, evaluation, safety guardrails, reliability, observability, cost, CI/CD regression tests, and human escalation.
sources.limitations: High-stakes clinical-agent specialization; clinicians and organizational authorities retain medical and risk decisions.

sources.title: Applied AI Engineer
sources.evidence_summary: Makes AI behavior measurable through system/behavior definitions, retrieval, evaluation, guardrails, adversarial/security testing, provider selection, versioning, regression testing, and translation of creative constraints into testable requirements.
sources.limitations: Entertainment-character specialization; prompt architecture is unusually central and not universal to all applied AI.

sources.title: Applied AI Engineer
sources.evidence_summary: Uses the title for design, build, evaluation, and deployment of enterprise AI systems spanning transformer/retrieval models, search, agent orchestration, assistants, production data pipelines, and secure integration.
sources.limitations: Enterprise service-management specialization and employer-specific architecture choices.

sources.title: Applied AI Engineer
sources.evidence_summary: Defines senior applied AI product development across multimodal search, understanding, generation, personalization, workflows, agents, modern data infrastructure, full-stack delivery, and polished user experience.
sources.limitations: Senior product role in one architecture/design marketplace; its visual/product sensibility is context-specific.

sources.title: AI Risk Management Framework
sources.author_or_org: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.evidence_summary: Provides voluntary lifecycle risk-management context for incorporating trustworthiness into the design, development, use, and evaluation of AI products, services, and systems.
sources.limitations: A cross-organizational framework, not a job definition or assignment of formal risk authority; AI RMF 1.0 is under revision.
sources.currentness: official framework with revision in progress

sources.title: AI Risk Management Framework FAQs
sources.author_or_org: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.evidence_summary: States that developers, users, and evaluators should consider validity, reliability, safety, security, resilience, accountability, transparency, privacy, and harmful-bias management across pre-design through deployment, use, testing, and evaluation.
sources.limitations: Defines lifecycle considerations rather than an engineer's unilateral authority or a complete implementation standard.
sources.currentness: official guidance; underlying framework under revision

sources.title: Applied AI Engineer (Fullstack), AI Co-Innovation
sources.evidence_summary: Combines full-stack AI product engineering, agent workflows, industrial data integration, customer deployment, UI work, enablement, and product feedback, demonstrating both title credibility and real overlap with FDE in some organizations.
sources.limitations: A deliberately customer-facing co-innovation role; its FDE-like engagement duties must not become universal Applied AI scope.

claims.statement: Applied AI Engineer is a current standalone title used across frontier labs, large technology employers, AI vendors, healthcare, entertainment, enterprise software, public sector, and product companies.
claims.limitations: The exact title is not standardized and aliases remain common.

claims.statement: The convergent lifecycle runs from use-case or task formulation through prototyping, application/system design, evaluation, production deployment, monitoring, and iteration.
claims.limitations: Customer discovery depth and ownership transfer vary by employer.

claims.statement: The role's distinctive technical problem is converting uncertain model capability into specified, measurable, and improvable behavior on real tasks.
claims.limitations: Behavior targets and evidence are domain-specific.

claims.statement: Production software and product engineering are core: applied AI work includes services, APIs, interfaces, schemas, orchestration, integration, deployment, and cross-stack debugging rather than prompt experimentation alone.
claims.limitations: Full-stack breadth and platform ownership vary by team.

claims.statement: Data, retrieval, context, tools, structured outputs, and deterministic integration boundaries are first-class parts of applied AI system behavior.
claims.limitations: Specific vector stores, frameworks, and APIs are replaceable implementation choices.

claims.statement: Evaluation is a core engineering loop spanning task datasets, quality criteria, failure taxonomy, regressions, edge cases, safety checks, online evidence, and feedback to model or system changes.
claims.limitations: No single grader or aggregate metric proves an AI system acceptable.

claims.statement: Production quality includes reliability, latency, cost, capacity, observability, recovery behavior, and safe degradation in addition to model-quality measures.
claims.limitations: Operational ownership may be shared with platform, MLOps, SRE, or product engineering teams.

claims.statement: Applied AI engineers implement and verify technical controls and risk evidence but do not thereby become legal, privacy, safety, security, clinical, audit, or organizational risk-acceptance authorities.
claims.limitations: Exact decision rights must be established by the organization and domain.

claims.statement: The unit of accountability is useful, safe-enough-for-authorized-use, measurable AI-powered product or system behavior for defined users and tasks—not an isolated model score.
claims.limitations: Business and formal risk decisions remain shared or external.

claims.statement: The durable role is broader than LLM applications: current evidence also includes traditional ML, multimodal systems, fine-tuning, search, recommendation, personalization, classification, and internal AI infrastructure.
claims.limitations: The current posting sample is heavily skewed toward generative and agentic AI.

claims.statement: Agentic AI engineering is a high-value Applied AI specialization, but agent planning, tool use, memory, permissions, autonomy, and recovery do not define every Applied AI Engineer role.
claims.limitations: Many 2026 postings foreground agents, so publication boundaries must actively prevent agent-only substitution.

claims.statement: Applied AI Engineer and Forward Deployed Engineer overlap when AI is delivered in customer environments, but the former centers AI system/product behavior while the latter centers the complete deployed customer outcome and engagement lifecycle.
claims.limitations: Some employers intentionally combine the roles; classification must use primary accountability rather than title alone.

claims.statement: Applied AI engineers collaborate with research and may reproduce, adapt, or fine-tune methods, but their center is turning capability into production behavior rather than creating generally novel model science.
claims.limitations: Frontier teams may deliberately blur research and engineering boundaries.

claims.statement: Applied AI engineering shares model/data work with machine learning engineering, but it is distinguished by application behavior, user/task evaluation, product integration, and end-to-end experience rather than generalized training/serving ownership.
claims.limitations: Many employers use AI Engineer, ML Engineer, and Applied ML Engineer interchangeably; responsibility evidence controls.

claims.statement: Applied AI architecture and solutions architecture emphasize design, feasibility, and guidance; the engineer role must implement, evaluate, ship, diagnose, and improve the running system.
claims.limitations: Hands-on architects and senior engineers can perform overlapping work.

claims.statement: The role usually expects experienced software/ML judgment, but seniority and specialization range from product-focused engineers to infrastructure, customer-facing, and industry-specific positions.
claims.limitations: Years-of-experience requirements are hiring filters, not a professional competency standard.

claims.statement: Advanced applied AI work creates reusable evaluation, behavior, integration, reliability, and governance mechanisms and communicates their limits, while roadmap priority and formal authorization remain with accountable partners.
claims.limitations: Platform and policy ownership varies by organization.
